Module 1.title: Thermal Power Plants & Supercritical Steam Cycles
Module 1.textbook_html:
MODULE 01 • S8 PROFESSIONAL ELECTIVE

Thermal Power Plants & Advanced Steam Cycles

Modern coal and gas-fired thermal power stations, Rankine cycle enhancements, reheat, regeneration, supercritical boilers, and cooling tower dynamics.

Key Learning Outcomes

  • Understand the working layout of modern high-capacity thermal power stations (500 MW - 800 MW units).
  • Formulate and analyze thermodynamic efficiencies of reheat, regenerative, and supercritical steam cycles.
  • Evaluate boiler feed water treatment, economizers, air preheaters, and electrostatic precipitators (ESP).
  • Compute condenser vacuum efficiency, cooling tower heat transfer rates, and overall thermal efficiency.

1. Modern Thermal Power Station Layout

A coal-fired thermal power station converts the chemical energy of coal into electrical power via a multi-stage energy conversion process: Combustion in boiler → High-pressure steam generation → Kinetic energy in steam turbines → Mechanical shaft rotation → Electrical power via alternator.

Figure 1.1: Detailed schematic of a pulverized coal thermal power plant showing boiler, superheater, reheat stages, turbine cylinder train (HP, IP, LP), condenser, feedwater preheaters, and cooling tower.
Source: Wikimedia Commons (Public Domain)

Key Station Subsystems:

  1. Coal and Ash Handling System: Wagon tipplers, stockyards, magnetic separators, bowl mills (pulverizers achieving 70% passing 200 mesh), bottom ash hoppers, and dry fly-ash pneumatic transport.
  2. Boiler & Air-Gas Circuit: Forced Draught (FD) fans push ambient air through rotary regenerative air preheaters; Primary Air (PA) fans transport pulverized coal; Induced Draught (ID) fans maintain balanced furnace draft (approx. -5 mm w.g.) discharging through 275 m tall multi-flue chimneys.
  3. Feedwater & Condensate Circuit: Deaerator for dissolved oxygen removal ($< 5 \; \text{ppb}$), Low-Pressure (LP) heaters, Boiler Feed Pumps (BFP delivering up to 300 bar), and High-Pressure (HP) heaters.

2. Supercritical & Ultra-Supercritical (USC) Cycles

Conventional subcritical units operate below the thermodynamic critical point of water ($T_c = 373.95^\circ\text{C}, P_c = 22.064 \; \text{MPa}$). In supercritical (SC) and ultra-supercritical (USC) plants, operating pressures reach 25–30 MPa with main and reheat steam temperatures of $600^\circ\text{C}$ to $620^\circ\text{C}$.

Rankine Cycle Thermal Efficiency with Reheat & Regeneration
$$\eta_{th} = \frac{W_{net}}{Q_{in}} = \frac{(h_1 - h_2) + (h_3 - h_4) - W_p}{(h_1 - h_{f6}) + (h_3 - h_2)}$$
Where $h_1$ is HP turbine inlet enthalpy, $h_2$ is cold reheat exit, $h_3$ is hot reheat entry, $h_4$ is LP turbine exhaust enthalpy, and $h_{f6}$ is economizer inlet enthalpy.

Step-by-Step Worked University Problem

Problem 1: In a 600 MW reheat steam cycle, steam enters the HP turbine at 170 bar and $540^\circ\text{C}$. After expansion to 40 bar, the steam is reheated to $540^\circ\text{C}$ and then expands in the IP/LP turbines to a condenser pressure of 0.07 bar. Neglecting pump work, calculate: (a) Cycle thermal efficiency, (b) Specific steam consumption (SSC) in kg/kWh.
Solution:

1. From Steam Tables:
State 1 ($170 \; \text{bar}, 540^\circ\text{C}$): $h_1 = 3395.3 \; \text{kJ/kg}, s_1 = 6.398 \; \text{kJ/kg}\cdot\text{K}$.
State 2s ($40 \; \text{bar}, s_{2s} = s_1$): $h_{2s} = 2960.5 \; \text{kJ/kg}$.
State 3 ($40 \; \text{bar}, 540^\circ\text{C}$): $h_3 = 3536.9 \; \text{kJ/kg}, s_3 = 7.185 \; \text{kJ/kg}\cdot\text{K}$.
State 4s ($0.07 \; \text{bar}$): $s_{4s} = 7.185 = s_f + x_4 s_{fg} = 0.559 + x_4 (7.717) \implies x_4 = 0.8586$.
$h_{4s} = h_f + x_4 h_{fg} = 163.4 + 0.8586(2409.1) = 2231.9 \; \text{kJ/kg}$.

2. Turbine Work:
$$W_T = (h_1 - h_{2s}) + (h_3 - h_{4s}) = (3395.3 - 2960.5) + (3536.9 - 2231.9) = 434.8 + 1305.0 = 1739.8 \; \text{kJ/kg}$$

3. Heat Supplied:
$$Q_{in} = (h_1 - h_{f4}) + (h_3 - h_{2s}) = (3395.3 - 163.4) + (3536.9 - 2960.5) = 3231.9 + 576.4 = 3808.3 \; \text{kJ/kg}$$

4. Thermal Efficiency & SSC:
$$\eta_{th} = \frac{W_T}{Q_{in}} = \frac{1739.8}{3808.3} = 45.68\%$$ $$\text{SSC} = \frac{3600}{W_T} = \frac{3600}{1739.8} = 2.069 \; \text{kg/kWh}$$

University & GATE Examination Questions

2 Marks
State the main advantage of supercritical steam power generation over subcritical units.
Supercritical units operate above critical pressure (no two-phase boiling pinch), boosting thermal efficiency from ~36% to 42–46%, reducing fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions by 15–20% per kWh produced.
8 Marks
Explain the operating principle and construction of an Electrostatic Precipitator (ESP) with a neat sketch.
ESP utilizes high negative DC voltage (40–70 kV) applied across discharge electrodes to create a corona discharge, ionizing flue gas molecules. Negative gas ions charge ash particles, which migrate toward grounded collecting plates and are dislodged by mechanical rapping into collection hoppers, achieving $> 99.8\%$ collection efficiency.

Module 2.title: Gas Turbine & Combined Cycle Power Plants
Module 2.textbook_html:
MODULE 02 • S8 PROFESSIONAL ELECTIVE

Gas Turbine & Combined Cycle Power Plants (CCPP)

Brayton-Rankine coupling, Heat Recovery Steam Generators (HRSG), gas turbine combustors, intercooling, reheating, and blade cooling physics.

1. Combined Cycle Gas Turbine (CCGT) Systems

A CCGT plant pairs a high-temperature Brayton cycle topping unit ($T_{in} \approx 1400^\circ\text{C}$–$1600^\circ\text{C}$) with a Rankine cycle bottoming unit utilizing the exhaust gas energy ($550^\circ\text{C}$–$620^\circ\text{C}$), achieving net station efficiencies exceeding 60%.

Combined Cycle Overall Thermal Efficiency
$$\eta_{cc} = \eta_b + \eta_r - (\eta_b \cdot \eta_r) = 1 - (1 - \eta_b)(1 - \eta_r)$$
Where $\eta_b$ is Brayton cycle efficiency and $\eta_r$ is Rankine bottoming efficiency.

Module 3.title: Nuclear Power Plants & Reactor Physics
Module 3.textbook_html:
MODULE 03 • S8 PROFESSIONAL ELECTIVE

Nuclear Power Plants & Reactor Physics

Nuclear fission cross-sections, neutron moderation, Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR), Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR), and nuclear waste encapsulation.

1. Nuclear Fission & Four-Factor Formula

Nuclear fission of $^{235}\text{U}$ by thermal neutrons ($E \approx 0.025 \; \text{eV}$) releases approximately $200 \; \text{MeV}$ of energy per fission event along with an average of 2.43 prompt neutrons.

Infinite Multiplication Factor ($k_\infty$)
$$k_\infty = \epsilon \cdot p \cdot f \cdot \eta$$
$\epsilon$ = fast fission factor, $p$ = resonance escape probability, $f$ = thermal utilization factor, $\eta$ = reproduction factor.

MODULE 04 • S8 PROFESSIONAL ELECTIVE

Solar, Wind & Renewable Energy Systems

Photovoltaic IV curves, MPPT algorithms, Betz limit aerodynamics for HAWT wind turbines, and hybrid microgrid stability.

1. Wind Power Aerodynamics & Betz Limit

Maximum Theoretical Wind Turbine Power (Betz Law)
$$P_{max} = \frac{16}{27} \left(\frac{1}{2} \rho A V^3\right) \approx 0.593 \cdot P_{wind}$$
Where $\rho$ is air density ($1.225 \; \text{kg/m}^3$), $A = \pi R^2$ is swept rotor area, and $V$ is upstream undisturbed wind velocity.

Module 5.title: Power Plant Economics, Load Curves & Environmental Impact
Module 5.textbook_html:
MODULE 05 • S8 PROFESSIONAL ELECTIVE

Power Economics & Environmental Management

Chronological load curves, load factor, diversity factor, tariff structures, Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE), and carbon capture technologies.

1. Power Economics Definitions

Key Power Plant Operational Factors
$$\text{Load Factor} = \frac{\text{Total Energy Generated (kWh)}}{\text{Peak Load (kW)} \times 8760 \; \text{hours}}$$ $$\text{Diversity Factor} = \frac{\sum \text{Individual Maximum Demands}}{\text{Coincident Maximum Station Demand}} > 1.0$$ $$\text{Capacity Factor} = \frac{\text{Actual Output (kWh)}}{\text{Installed Capacity (kW)} \times 8760 \; \text{hours}}$$
